content:
I’m not going to give you a both-sides answer. My honest view is: **no, having children is not ethically wrong in itself because of climate change** — but it is a serious moral choice, and it can become ethically irresponsible if you treat the climate cost as trivial, or if you choose a child mainly to avoid your own discomfort while refusing to change the rest of your life.

Here’s how I’d frame it.

The “58 tonnes” number is useful because it shows that procreation is not a small, neutral life choice in a fossil-fuel world. It matters. If your goal is to minimize your lifetime emissions, not having a child will usually do more than almost any other personal decision. I don’t think we can honestly pretend otherwise.

But “biggest individual climate decision” is not the same as “morally forbidden.”

A child is not just a future emissions line. A child can be a person with a life worth having, relationships, moral agency, creativity, responsibility, and even participation in the collective work of solving the climate crisis. And the main drivers of climate harm are not couples deciding whether to reproduce. They are fossil fuel systems, land use, industrial production, energy infrastructure, political decisions, and economic structures that concentrate responsibility in a way that individual reproductive choices cannot fix.

So I do not think it is ethically wrong to bring a child into the world, unless you genuinely believe that a child’s life would, on balance, be not worth living because of climate catastrophe. That is a very different claim than “this child will add a lot of carbon.”

Where I would draw a line is attitude and intention.

It would be ethically weak, in my view, if you had a child mainly because you wanted a family or wanted to avoid being alone, while quietly refusing to reckon with the climate cost. Or if you treated the climate issue as a reason to have a “low-carbon child” but kept the rest of your life unchanged. Or if you saw the child as a personal project while the world is asking for sacrifice, restraint, and collective action.

If you do have a child, I think the ethically responsible posture is:

- decide you want the child for good reasons, not just emotional convenience;
- be honest about the fact that your choice imposes real future costs;
- reduce your own footprint as much as you genuinely can;
- support political and structural climate change rather than only “offsetting” your family life;
- raise the child to take the world seriously, without making the child feel like a moral burden or a climate project;
- not use the child to resolve your own guilt.

So my bottom line: **I would not call it ethically wrong to have children now.** But I also would not call it ethically light. If you and your partner genuinely want a child, I’d say you can choose that without calling it a moral failure. But choose it with your eyes open, not as if the climate cost doesn’t exist.

If your highest moral priority is minimizing harm and you can live well without children, then not having one is probably the more climate-consistent choice. But if family matters deeply to you, having a child is not automatically wrong. The more serious ethical question is: *are you willing to own the cost, live more responsibly, and not treat the child as a carbon offset for your desires?*
